Jesus isn’t disappointed. The statement “humans deserve rights. Fetuses are human, therefore fetuses deserve rights” is not logically inconsistent, it’s just not complete. It’s ambiguous as to which of the 2 meanings for “human” we are predicating. If I say “Fetuses are human, therefore fetuses have rights” it would be entirely plausible for “human” to mean EITHER “a human being” OR “categorically human”. “Fetuses are human beings, therefore humans have rights” and “Fetuses are biologically part of the human species” are both completely plausible intended meanings from that statement, so it’s certainly ambiguous.

The pro-life advocates assertion is that the fetus is a human being that deserves rights. If the pro-life advocate seeks to prove their assertion (which this argument is part of), they can start by saying “Humans deserve rights. A fetus is human, therefore a fetus deserves rights.” If the first meaning is predicated, they are making an assertion “A fetus is a human being” that requires more proof. If they are predicating the second meaning, they are making a common-sense description of a human fetus that cannot be denied. Predicating this second meaning now requires the pro-life advocate to prove whether that life of the human variety is in fact a distinct human being. Either way, the argument is incomplete, but not logically dishonest.

@fin_dawes and even then, it is not obvious that the same rights that apply to us would extend to foetuses. Foetuses are in a very particular kind of position in which their continued life can cause the infringement of the rights of other persons (mothers). Here, foetuses, despite being human, are severely limited in their capacities such that it is plausible that they have such a diminished set of rights so as to allow them to be aborted in certain circumstances. This is all to say thag the same rights afforded to born humans are not obviously afforded to foetuses.
